title: ClickFix has never been bigger, and AI tools are its most convincing lure yet
description: ClickFix is a rapidly growing browser-based attack technique that uses fake AI tool installers, malicious search results, and trusted chatbot platforms to trick users into executing malware. Attackers exploit user habits around AI tool adoption, such as running terminal install commands and searching for AI apps via search engines, to deliver malicious payloads. These attacks bypass traditional defenses by leveraging legitimate domains, cloaking, and in-memory execution. ClickFix attacks accounted for up to 67% of detected browser-based attacks in mid-2026, with a significant portion delivered through compromised websites, malvertising, and SEO poisoning. Variants like InstallFix and LLMshare use cloned install pages and malicious shared AI chatbot artifacts to lure victims. Microsoft reports ClickFix as a highly effective initial access technique with over 1.1 million unique devices affected in early 2026.
aiSummary: ClickFix is a family of browser-based attack techniques that have surged since 2024, now comprising a majority of detected browser attacks. The attacks use fake AI tool installers and malicious search results to trick users into running commands that deliver malware directly in memory, evading endpoint detection. Attackers exploit common AI adoption behaviors, such as copying terminal install commands from web pages and searching for AI tools via search engines, to deliver malicious payloads. Techniques include InstallFix, which clones legitimate install pages but replaces commands with malicious ones, and LLMshare, which abuses AI chatbot sharing features to host malicious instructions or links on trusted AI platforms. The attacks use cloaking, compromised legitimate sites, and blockchain-based payload configuration to evade detection and takedown. Microsoft Defender observed over 1.1 million unique devices executing ClickFix commands in early 2026, with a 96.3% malware conversion rate.
aiImpact: ClickFix attacks lead to widespread malware infections by tricking users into executing malicious commands in legitimate shells, bypassing email security, URL reputation checks, and endpoint detection. The attacks have infected over a million devices in early 2026 alone, with a high success rate of malware delivery. The use of legitimate domains, compromised websites, and AI platforms for hosting lures complicates detection and mitigation. The attacks enable initial access for further compromise and malware deployment.
